passages.title: The Science Behind Why Fireworks Have Different Colors
passages.text: There is nothing quite like watching a fireworks display, the loud booms, the dazzling sparks, and, most mesmerising, the brilliant colours lighting up the sky. But have you ever wondered why fireworks have different colours? The secret lies in chemistry! Fireworks get their vibrant hues from metal salts and chemical compounds that emit specific colours when heated. How Do Fireworks Produce Colours? At the heart of every firework is a carefully crafted chemical mixture. When ignited, these chemicals undergo exothermic reactions, releasing energy through light and heat. The colours we see depend on the metal ions present in the compounds. The Role of Metal Salts in Firework Colours When burned, different metals produce different colours due to atomic emission spectra, a phenomenon where excited electrons release energy as light at specific wavelengths. Here’s how it works: 1. Heat excites electrons in metal atoms, causing them to jump to higher energy levels. 2. As the electrons return to their original state, they release energy as light. 3. passages.text: Blog The Chemistry of Fireworks: Why Different Metals Burn Different Colours Every fireworks display is, fundamentally, a controlled demonstration of redox chemistry. The bright reds, greens, blues and golds you see lighting up the night sky aren’t just pretty colours — they’re the direct result of electrons jumping between energy levels in metal ions. And if you’re studying A Level Chemistry, understanding why different metals burn different colours is not just fascinating — it’s essential exam knowledge. What Makes Fireworks Burn at All? At its heart, a firework is a fuel (usually a finely powdered metal or metal compound) mixed with an oxidising agent, bound together and ignited. The reaction is violent because it releases enormous amounts of energy very quickly. For a firework to work, you need three things: - A fuel: usually a metal powder (sodium, potassium, strontium, copper, barium, etc.) - An oxidising agent: typically potassium nitrate (KNO3) or potassium perchlorate - Heat: a spark or fuse to initiate the reaction The reaction between the metal and the oxidising agent is highly exothermic — it releases a lot of energy. For example, a ring of stars creates a circular burst. 2. Are fireworks bad for the environment? Traditional fireworks release smoke and metal particles, which can contribute to air pollution. Some companies now make eco-friendly fireworks with cleaner-burning materials. 3. Can fireworks be any color? Almost! Fireworks can reach temperatures of 1,000–1,600°C (1,800–3,000°F), hot enough to excite metal ions and produce bright colours. 5. Who invented colored fireworks? Early fireworks (invented in China around 1,000 years ago) were mostly orange and white. Italian pyrotechnicians in the 1830s discovered that metal salts could produce different colours. Conclusion: The Brilliant Chemistry of Fireworks Next time you watch a fireworks show, you’ll know the science behind those dazzling colours. Each hue comes from a carefully chosen metal compound reacting to heat. From the deep reds of strontium to the elusive blues of copper, fireworks are a perfect blend of chemistry, physics, and artistry.

Not all fireworks colours are equally easy to produce. Here’s why: - Blue is the toughest: Copper compounds require very precise temperatures to emit a true blue. Too hot, and the colour fades; too cool, and it looks greenish. - Green and red are easier: Barium and strontium compounds are more stable, producing vibrant colours reliably. - Purple is a mix: Since no single element creates deep purple, pyrotechnicians blend red (strontium) and blue (copper) compounds. How Are Fireworks Designed for Different Effects? Beyond colours, fireworks can create shapes, patterns, and even sounds! Here’s how: - Stars: Small pellets of colour-producing chemicals arranged in patterns (like hearts or smiley faces). - Crackling effects: Made with lead or bismuth oxides that create tiny explosions. - Whistling sounds: Are created by tubes that force out gases at high speeds. The Chemistry of Specific Colours Red and Crimson: Strontium (Sr) Strontium produces the classic red/crimson colour in fireworks. When strontium atoms burn, their electrons jump to higher energy levels and then fall back, releasing photons with a wavelength around 640 nm — right in the red part of the visible spectrum. Redox equation: 2Sr + O2 → 2SrO Strontium is in Group 2 of the periodic table, so it readily loses two electrons to form Sr2+ ions. The oxidation state of strontium changes from 0 to +2. This is oxidation — loss of electrons. Green: Barium (Ba) Barium compounds produce the brilliant green colour you see in fireworks. The energy gap for barium’s excited electrons produces photons around 500–550 nm — green light. Redox equation: 2Ba + O2 → 2BaO Like strontium, barium is also in Group 2, so it loses two electrons: Ba → Ba2+ + 2e– Blue: Copper (Cu) Copper salts produce bright blue colours. Why Do Different Metals Produce Different Colours? This is where the real chemistry comes in, and it’s directly linked to the energy levels in atoms. When electrons in an atom absorb energy, they jump from a lower energy level to a higher one. This is called excitation. The excited electron is unstable and quickly falls back down to its original level, releasing the energy it absorbed as a photon (a particle of light). The colour of the light depends on the energy of the photon. Different amounts of energy produce different colours: - Lower energy → red light - Higher energy → blue/violet light Because different metal atoms have different electron configurations, the energy gaps between their electron levels are different. So when their electrons fall back down, they release different amounts of energy, producing different colours. The tightly packed composition burns in an oscillating fashion, forcing gas out of the tube opening in rapid pulses. The confinement tube acts as a resonating cavity, similar to a flute, amplifying these pulses into the characteristic high-pitched whistle. The specific pitch can be adjusted by altering the internal diameter and length of the tube. Crackling effects, often called “dragon eggs,” are achieved using small granules of pyrotechnic mixture that contain compounds like bismuth trioxide or lead tetroxide. These granules are designed to burn for a short duration before undergoing a secondary, delayed micro-explosion, resulting in a series of rapid, sharp pops and flashes. Other specialized effects, like a rapid-fire strobe, use a composition that burns in an alternating manner, creating a momentary flickering light instead of a sustained burn.

passages.text: Fireworks colors are a result of chemistry in action. The colors come partly from the elements and compounds used in fireworks and partly by incandescence or light produced by different temperatures. Here’s a look at how fireworks produce their brilliant hues. Key Takeaways – Firework Colors - Firework colors come from chemical luminescence (excited metal ions) and incandescence (heated materials). - Each color is tied to a specific element or compound. - Purity and temperature are critical to getting vivid, accurate colors. - Watching fireworks becomes even more exciting when you know the chemistry behind each burst. Firework Colors – Luminescence of Element and Compounds When chemicals are heated, the ions emit characteristic wavelengths or colors of light—a phenomenon known as luminescence. This is the same principle behind the classic flame test used in chemistry labs. In fireworks, heating metal salts and other compounds excites their electrons, which then release energy in the form of visible light. Each element produces its own distinct color. Many firework colors are created through luminescence, but bright white and gold sparks rely on incandescence. Incandescence is light produced by heating a material to a very high temperature, causing it to glow. Metals like aluminum, magnesium, and titanium burn intensely hot, creating dazzling white and silver light. The combination of these two mechanisms—element-specific luminescence and heat-dependent incandescence—allows for a vast palette of pyrotechnic color. Engineering the Shape: How Stars Create Patterns Beyond the chemical composition, the physical structure inside the firework shell determines the shape of the burst. The shell is a cardboard sphere or cylinder packed with “stars” and a central black powder charge, known as the bursting charge. The key to creating a specific pattern lies in the precise arrangement of the stars around this central explosive core. For common effects, like the spherical peony or chrysanthemum, the stars are symmetrically packed and propelled outward evenly. After all, fireworks are explosives, and working with them is best left to the professionals. Bottom line: The red, orange, yellow, green, blue and purple colors exploding in the night sky during a fireworks festival are created by the use of metal salts. For example, trace sodium contamination may produce intense yellow light that masks red or green effects. Firework Colors – Incandescence Not all firework colors come from chemical luminescence. Some result from incandescence—the light emitted by materials as they get hot. You’ve likely seen this in action with a stove burner: dark when cold, glowing red when hot, and bright white when extremely hot. In fireworks, incandescent effects are used for glowing sparks, glitter trails, and brilliant flashes. Common metals such as iron, titanium, and aluminum are used for these effects. Their color depends on both the temperature and the particle size: - Titanium: brilliant white sparks with longer trails - Iron sparks: yellow-orange - Aluminum: white flashes and silver sparks Firework Periodic Table Want a quick reference? When ignited, the rapid combustion of this powder generates a high volume of gas, propelling the shell skyward with significant force. Attached to the shell is a time fuse, which is ignited simultaneously with the lift charge. This fuse burns as the shell ascends, acting as a countdown timer to the desired altitude. The length and chemical composition of the time fuse are calculated to ensure the interior bursting charge detonates exactly at the shell’s apex before it begins to fall. Different firework types use varying amounts of lift charge and fuse lengths to control trajectory and delay. A longer fuse and larger lift charge send a shell higher, while a short delay and smaller charge result in effects closer to the ground. Controlling these two mechanical elements ensures the entire display is a synchronized sequence of bursts.
